issues.legal_issue: An arbitral finding that an existing legal regime permitted royalty to be included as a tariff cost, and that later measures changed that regime, is perverse when it is unsupported by evidence and ignores material tariff decisions.
material_facts: The bid, financial offer and letter of intent preceded the relevant tariff guidelines.
The initial tariff decision expressly left royalty-related issues unresolved and disclaimed any implicit approval of royalty treatment.
A later tariff decision specifically refused to treat royalty as an admissible tariff cost.
The arbitral tribunal nevertheless found that royalty had previously been permitted as a pass-through and that later measures changed the law.
The award did not take account of the material tariff decisions.
issues.conclusion: The tribunal’s finding of a change in law was based on no evidence and ignored vital evidence, making it perverse and patent illegality on the face of the award; the award was therefore liable to be set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 34(2)(b)(ii) and 34(2-A) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, as amended, a domestic award may be set aside for patent illegality appearing on its face, including a perverse finding based on no evidence or one that ignores vital evidence. Mere erroneous application of law or reappreciation of evidence is not enough. Sections 34 and 37 do not permit merits review. The Court relied on MMTC Limited v. Vedanta Limited, Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority, and Ssangyong Engineering and Construction Company Limited v. National Highways Authority of India.

predicates.domestic_arbitral_award_challenged: A party challenged a domestic arbitral award through the statutory process for setting aside an award and any appeal from that decision.
predicates.finding_based_on_no_evidence: The arbitrator made a material finding without evidence supporting it.
predicates.finding_ignores_vital_evidence: The arbitrator made a material finding without taking account of evidence essential to the decision.

issues.definition: If a challenged domestic award contains a material finding unsupported by evidence or reached by ignoring vital evidence, the award may be set aside for patent illegality.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitral tribunal cannot unilaterally replace an agreed contractual payment method with a different method opposed by a contracting party.
material_facts: The agreement required the operator to pay royalty calculated by reference to minimum guaranteed traffic.
The operator sought to change the agreement from a royalty payment method to a revenue-sharing method.
The port authority opposed that change and did not consent to replacing the agreed method.
The tribunal substituted a revenue-sharing method for the royalty method, including setting a revenue-share percentage.
issues.conclusion: The tribunal was not justified in substituting the royalty method with the revenue-sharing method; the award imposed a new contract without the consent of the opposing party and was patent illegality.
issues.legal_principle: An arbitrator must act within the four corners of the agreement and cannot impose a unilateral alteration or make a party perform a bargain it did not accept. Such rewriting may breach fundamental principles of justice and amount to patent illegality under Section 34(2-A) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The Court relied on Ssangyong Engineering and Construction Company Limited v. National Highways Authority of India, Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. v. Annapurna Construction, and Md. Army Welfare Housing Organization v. Sumangal Services (P) Ltd.

predicates.domestic_arbitral_award_challenged: A party challenged a domestic arbitral award through the statutory process for setting aside an award and any appeal from that decision.
predicates.arbitrator_replaces_agreed_contract_term: The arbitrator substituted a contractual term with a different term that the parties had not agreed to.
predicates.other_party_did_not_consent: The other contracting party opposed the substituted term and did not agree to the change.

issues.definition: If a challenged domestic award substitutes an agreed contractual term with a different term without the other party’s consent, the award may be set aside for unilateral rewriting of the contract.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal under Section 37 cannot enlarge the court’s review beyond the grounds and limits applicable to an application under Section 34.
material_facts: The arbitral award was challenged under Section 34 and the resulting decision was appealed under Section 37.
The dispute before the Court concerned whether the award could be set aside on the statutory grounds, including patent illegality.
issues.conclusion: A court hearing an appeal under Section 37 cannot independently reassess the merits of the award or exceed the restrictions applicable under Section 34.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 34 and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a court does not sit in appeal over the award or reappreciate evidence; review under Section 37 cannot travel beyond the limits of Section 34. The Court relied on MMTC Limited v. Vedanta Limited, Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority, and Ssangyong Engineering and Construction Company Limited v. National Highways Authority of India.

predicates.appeal_from_section_34_decision: A party brought an appeal from a court’s decision on an application to set aside an arbitral award.
predicates.court_reassesses_award_merits: The appellate court independently reexamined the merits or evidence underlying the arbitral award.

issues.definition: When a court hears an appeal from a decision on an award challenge, it cannot independently reassess the award’s merits beyond the limits governing the original challenge.
